title: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Solubility of calcium salts in colloids”. Scope: calcified tissues of animals, especially bone and calcareous skeletons

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-06: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.44

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The chemical mechanism has measurable variables and experimentally separable rivals. However, suitable paired kinetic data appear unlikely to exist openly, and extrapolation from simplified solutions to all calcified tissues would remain inadequate.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure calcium carbonate and phosphate solubility and precipitation kinetics as intact albumins are enzymatically degraded, while controlling pH, carbonate and competing ions. Support requires protein breakdown to precede and quantitatively explain mineral precipitation better than direct acid-base chemistry.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
In vivo calcification includes active ion transport and specialized matrix proteins.

Public datasets rarely combine proteolysis kinetics with mineral supersaturation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The chemical alternative is clear enough to test in vitro and at a mineralization front, but the needed paired measurements are not in an open resource. Older solubility remarks are scattered in the chemical literature and do not cover skeletal tissues at the stated scope. Discriminating the protein-breakdown route from carbonic-acid precipitation, among other controls now known to matter, would require new compiled measurements.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare calcium carbonate and phosphate solubility in intact albumin versus its breakdown products, and test whether mineralization fronts in calcified tissues coincide with proteolysis rather than with carbonic-acid reaction on a more soluble salt. Precipitation tied to protein breakdown, and not to the acid route, would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern mineralization also depends on phosphate supply and inhibitors, which the two historical mechanisms do not capture.

No public dataset pairs local proteolysis, protein concentration and mineral appearance in calcifying tissues.
